benchmark_text: People can keep track of some things, seeing where they come from and where they go.
Objects change in some ways and stay the same in some ways.

No matter how parts of an object are assembled, the weight of the whole object is always the same as the sum of the parts; and when an object is broken into parts, the parts have the same total weight as the original object.
The number of objects in a group can stay the same even as some come or leave as long as each one that leaves is replaced by another one that is entering.
No matter how substances within a closed system interact with one another, or how they combine or break apart, the total mass of the system remains the same.
The amount of something in a system may stay the same because nothing is entering or leaving the system or because something is being added to the system at the same rate as it is leaving the system.
Whatever happens within a system, such as parts exploding, decaying, or reorganizing, some features, such as the total amount of matter and energy, remain precisely the same.

The amount of something in a system may stay the same because nothing is happening to it or because it is being transformed into something else at the same rate as something else is being transformed into it.
A system may stay the same because nothing is influencing it or the influences on it are balanced.
Many systems contain feedback mechanisms that serve to keep changes within certain limits.
Even though a system may appear to be unchanging when viewed macroscopically, there is continual activity of the molecules in the system.

If a system in equilibrium is disturbed, it may return to a very similar state of equilibrium, or it may undergo a radical change until the system achieves a new state of equilibrium with very different conditions, or it may fail to achieve any type of equilibrium.
An object can change in various ways, such as in size, weight, color, or temperature.
Some things, such as a persons age, change in only one direction.
Things change in steady, repetitive, or erratic ways—or sometimes in more than one way at the same time.
Trends based on what has happened in the past can be used to make predictions about what things will be like in the future. However, these predictions may not always match what actually happens.
Trends that follow a pattern that can be described mathematically can be used to estimate how long a process has been going on.
The present arises from the conditions of the past and, in turn, affects what is possible in the future.
The way some systems behave is so erratic that patterns of change are not apparent.

Small differences in how things start out can sometimes produce large differences in how they end up. Some events are so sensitive to small differences in initial conditions that their outcomes cannot be predicted.
Cyclic patterns evident in past events can be used to make predictions about future events. However, these predictions may not always match what actually happens.

Most systems above the molecular level involve so many parts that it is not practical to determine the existing conditions and thus the precise behavior of every part of the system cannot be predicted.
The precise future of a system is not completely determined by its present state and circumstances but also depends on the fundamentally uncertain outcomes of events on the atomic scale.
Some things in nature have a repeating pattern, such as the day-night cycle, the phases of the moon, and seasons.

Cycles, such as the seasons or body temperature, can be described by what their cycle length or frequency is, what their highest and lowest values are, and when these values occur. Different cycles range from many years down to a fraction of a second.
Cyclic change is commonly found when there are feedback effects in a system—as, for example, when a change in any direction gives rise to forces or influences that oppose the change.
People can keep track of some things, seeing where they come from and where they go.
Some things change so slowly or so quickly that the changes are hard to notice while they are taking place.
Small changes can sometimes be detected by comparing counts or measurements at different times.
Often the best way to tell which kinds of change are happening is to make a graph of measurements.
Graphical display of quantities may make it possible to spot patterns that are not otherwise obvious, such as cycles and trends.
The graphic display of numbers may help to show patterns such as trends, varying rates of change, gaps, or clusters that are useful when making predictions about the phenomena being graphed.
Symbolic equations can be used to summarize how the quantity of something changes over time or in response to other changes.
Graphs and equations are useful (and often equivalent) ways for depicting and analyzing patterns of change.

It is not always easy to recognize meaningful patterns of change in a set of data. Data that appear to be completely irregular may be shown by statistical analysis to have underlying trends or cycles.
All materials have certain physical properties, such as strength, hardness, flexibility, durability, resistance to water and fire, and ease of conducting heat.
A substance has characteristic properties, such as density, a boiling point, and solubility, all of which are independent of the amount of the substance and can be used to identify it.
Some properties of an object depend on its length, some depend on its area, and some depend on its volume.

When the linear dimensions of an object change by some factor, its area and volume change disproportionately: area in proportion to the square of the factor, and volume in proportion to its cube. Properties of an object that depend on its area or volume also change disproportionately.
Because different properties are not affected to the same degree by changes in size, large changes in size typically change the way that things work in physical, biological, or social systems.
Both shape and scale can have important consequences for the performance of systems.
Things in nature and things people make have very different sizes, weights, ages, and speeds.

Natural phenomena often involve sizes, durations, and speeds that are extremely small or extremely large. These phenomena may be difficult to appreciate because they involve magnitudes far outside human experience.
Use whole numbers in ordering, counting, identifying, measuring, and describing objects and events.
Finding out what the largest and the smallest values of something are is often as informative as knowing what the usual value is.
Express numbers like 100, 1,000, and 1,000,000 as powers of ten.
Representing very large or very small numbers in terms of powers of ten makes it easier to perform calculations using those numbers.
When describing and comparing very small and very large quantities, express them using powers-of-ten notation.
